title: When you buy a stock, what do you actually own?
subtitle: Not just a line of numbers on a screen - but a real economic right
openingQuestion: You own 0.001% of a company's shares. What does that really mean?
openingOptions: Owning stock has nothing to do with the company's real assets
You only own the right to resell the stock to someone else
You genuinely own 0.001% of the company's profit, net assets, and voting rights - a small ratio, but a real and quantifiable right
Just a fictional number in your brokerage account, with no real-world meaning
explanation: Owning stock means owning a proportional share in: (1) the company's net assets; (2) its stream of future profit; (3) voting rights on major decisions (electing the board, mergers...). The price on the screen is just the market's expression of these real economic rights. Because these three rights are what really matters, purely accounting moves like a stock split or reverse stock split - which only change the number of shares and the price per share by an agreed ratio - do not change a shareholder's actual ownership percentage or economic value at all, just like exchanging a 100,000-dong note for ten 10,000-dong notes doesn't make you richer or poorer.

realWorldExample.description: Even holding just a few shares, an individual investor still has the right to attend and vote at the annual shareholder meeting - this right applies in proportion to the number of shares held, however small.

quiz.question: Why can two investors holding the same number of shares in two different companies end up with very different real economic value?
options: Because the price per share of the two companies isn't the same
Because the two companies apply different accounting standards
Because the same share count represents very different ownership stakes
Because one of the two companies may never have paid a dividend
quiz.explanation: 100 shares of a company with a $10 billion market cap carries entirely different economic value from 100 shares of a company with a $10 million market cap - because the real ownership stake in assets and profit is very different. This is why you shouldn't look only at the 'number of shares owned' without understanding the ratio and value of the company behind it.

quiz.question: A company with 1 billion shares outstanding decides on a 10:1 reverse stock split, turning 1 billion shares into 100 million shares while each share's price rises tenfold. What happens to each shareholder's real ownership ratio and economic value?
options: Ownership ratio stays the same but total value falls
Ownership ratio falls tenfold but value stays the same
Each shareholder's value rises tenfold along with the share price
Nothing at all changes, only the unit of measurement changes
quiz.explanation: A reverse stock split or a regular stock split only changes the "unit of measurement" (the number of shares and the price per share) without changing the real ownership ratio or the company's total value - a clear demonstration that "what you own" matters far more than the surface-level share count.

quiz.question: What does holding 1% of a company's shares mean economically?
options: The right to 1% of the net assets and 1% of the profit of the company
The right to receive 1% of the company's annual revenue
The right to demand the company buy back your shares at any time
The right to run one percent of the company's operations
quiz.explanation: Owning shares means owning a proportional share of net assets and profit, not of revenue. Revenue still has to have every expense subtracted before anything belongs to shareholders.

quiz.question: Why doesn't a price of 200,000 dong per share mean that stock is expensive?
options: Because the share price is always adjusted for inflation each year
Because the price per share depends on how many shares it's been split into
Because a high price usually comes with low liquidity, making it hard to compare
Because high-priced stocks usually belong to larger companies
quiz.explanation: The same business split into 10 million or 1 billion shares gives two prices that differ a hundredfold with no change in value at all. Expensive or cheap has to be measured with a multiple like P/E, not an absolute number.

quiz.question: How does a 2:1 stock split affect a shareholder?
options: The share count stays the same but the ownership ratio doubles
The share count doubles and so does the total value held
The share count doubles, the price halves, value stays the same
The share count doubles and the company must raise more capital
quiz.explanation: Cutting a cake into more slices doesn't make the cake bigger. A split mainly makes the price per share more accessible to small investors - it creates no value at all.

keyTakeaways: Owning stock = owning a proportional share of the assets, profit, and voting rights
The share price is just the market's expression of the real economic right underneath
The number of shares owned means nothing when separated from the company's scale and value

practicePrompt.question: You own 0.001% of a listed company's shares. Besides the right to receive dividends (if declared), what other specific rights do you hold as a shareholder, even with such a tiny ownership stake?
options: Only the right to receive dividends - no other right, since the ownership stake is too small to matter
Owning shares means owning a proportional claim on assets, profits and voting rights
Only the right to resell the shares on the exchange - no right at all related to the company's assets or governance
Shareholder rights only arise once the ownership stake reaches at least 5%
practicePrompt.explanation: Owning stock = owning a proportional share of the assets, profit, and voting rights - even at a very small ratio, you legally still hold all three of these basic rights, only the degree of influence on company decisions is negligible compared to a large shareholder.

summary.keyIdea: Owning stock = owning a proportional share of the assets, profit, and voting rights
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: The share price is just the market's expression of the real economic right underneath

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: For a stock you're interested in, try finding its latest financial statement and estimating the net assets and profit the company generates that correspond to the ownership ratio you have (or plan to buy).
application.secondary: This exercise helps you see beyond the flickering price number on the screen.

sections.text: When you tap the buy button on an app, what you actually get isn't just a number in your account - it's a real ownership ratio in the assets, future profit, and voice of a business.

Owning stock means owning a proportional share of: (1) the company's net assets - factories, cash, inventory minus debt; (2) the profit the company will generate in the future; (3) voting rights on major decisions like electing the board or approving mergers. The price on the screen is just how the market 'prices' these three layers of right at a given moment - it can drift away from real value, but that doesn't change the nature of the ownership right underneath.
The number of shares alone tells you nothing

100 shares of a company with a 10,000-billion-dong market cap carries completely different economic value from 100 shares of a company with a 10-billion-dong market cap - because the real ownership stake in assets and profit is very different. Similarly, when a company does a 10:1 reverse stock split - turning 1 billion shares into 100 million shares with the price per share rising tenfold - each shareholder's ownership ratio and economic value doesn't change at all. It's just exchanging ten 10,000-dong notes for one 100,000-dong note, making no one richer or poorer.

items: Real economic value = ownership ratio × company value, not the absolute number of shares
A stock split or reverse split only changes the 'unit of measurement', neither creating nor destroying value
Voting rights apply proportionally to the number of shares held, even for a small retail investor with just a few shares
Always ask 'what percentage of this company do I own' rather than just looking at the number of shares

lines: Don't count shares - measure your ownership ratio. That's what actually decides how much of the business you really have.
